items.title: EEG-based sentiment & brain-state tracking (CNEL × Sony × LB3 dataset)
items.subtitle: End-to-end pipeline that cleans raw EEG and learns a compact, time-evolving ‘hidden state’ summary that can be evaluated against labels and behavioral outcomes.
items.imgAlt: Diagram showing an EEG modeling pipeline.
items.desc: Pipeline that turns brain-wave recordings (EEG) into a small set of hidden time-series ‘states’ using a state-space model (Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System, HLDS), then evaluates those states for prediction and separability.

details.overview: In this work, I focused on making brain-signal modeling practical: take raw EEG recordings collected while participants view media, clean and standardize them, fit a time-series model that tracks a few hidden variables over time, and produce clear metrics and reports so results are comparable across sessions and subjects.
what_i_built: A reproducible data pipeline (loading → cleaning → segmentation → feature preparation) that turns raw EEG into model-ready inputs.
Training and evaluation scripts for a state-space model called a Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System (HLDS), used to track hidden ‘brain state’ trajectories.
Diagnostics and scoring outputs (e.g., stability checks, prediction metrics, and class/condition separability summaries).
Automated summaries and artifacts so runs can be audited and compared (configuration capture, standardized outputs, and plots).
how_it_works: EEG is cleaned and aligned into consistent time windows.
The HLDS model learns hidden variables that evolve over time and explain the observed EEG signals.
Those hidden variables (and model outputs) are evaluated against labels/conditions to test whether the model captures meaningful structure.
deliverables: Run folders with configs, logs, metrics, and plots.
A standardized summary table used for comparison across papers/conditions.
collaborators: Computational NeuroEngineering Lab (CNEL), University of Florida
Sony Research collaboration (dataset and research context)

writeup.lead: This project turns messy EEG recordings into a compact, moving summary of brain state that you can actually evaluate.

sections.heading: What problem is this solving?
body: EEG is cheap, non-invasive, and extremely noisy. When you record it while someone watches media, the interesting structure — how a person's internal state shifts over time — is buried under muscle artifacts, drift, and large differences from one subject to the next. The goal here is to recover a small number of hidden variables that track that state cleanly enough to test against labels.
The emphasis is on *practical* brain-signal modeling: not a demo that works on one clean recording, but a pipeline that stays honest across sessions and subjects.

sections.heading: Why a state-space model?
body: Rather than throw a large black-box network at the raw signal, I use a Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System (HLDS). It assumes the EEG is generated by a few latent variables that evolve smoothly over time, and that assumption is a feature rather than a limitation: the hidden states stay interpretable, the model needs far less data than a deep network, and you can directly inspect whether the learned dynamics are stable.
When the question is what the brain is doing over time, a model whose internal variables you can read is worth more than a slightly higher benchmark number you cannot explain.

figure.alt: Diagram of a state-space model: a few hidden states evolving over time generate the many observed EEG channels above them.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — The state-space view: a small chain of hidden states evolves over time and generates the many noisy EEG channels we actually record.

sections.heading: How the model is trained and used
body: The HLDS runs in two clearly separated phases. In training, it learns its parameters with a dual-Kalman-filter procedure: it alternates between inferring the hidden states and updating the model parameters, repeating over multiple passes through the data. At inference time those parameters are frozen, and a Kalman-style recursion runs bottom-up to infer the hidden-state trajectory for a new recording. Those trajectories become the compact encodings the classifier reads.
Splitting learning from inference this way is what keeps evaluation honest: the encodings a downstream classifier sees are produced under fixed parameters, not quietly re-fit to each test recording.

figure.alt: Two-phase HLDS: training alternates hidden-state inference and parameter updates over multiple passes to learn parameters; inference freezes those parameters and runs a Kalman recursion to produce hidden-state encodings for a classifier.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — Training learns the parameters with a dual-Kalman loop; inference freezes them and runs a Kalman recursion to turn a new recording into hidden-state encodings for the classifier.

sections.heading: The pipeline around the model
body: Each experiment is a fixed sequence of stages, so a result from one subject or session can be compared fairly against another:

breakdown.label: Preprocessing
breakdown.text: Clean, standardize, and align raw recordings into consistent time windows the model can consume.

breakdown.label: Training
breakdown.text: Fit the HLDS parameters with the dual-Kalman procedure over multiple passes.

breakdown.label: Post-processing
breakdown.text: Turn inferred states into the encodings and summaries used downstream.

breakdown.label: Classification
breakdown.text: Evaluate how well those encodings predict and separate the conditions of interest.

breakdown.label: Analysis (EDA)
breakdown.text: Stability checks, diagnostics, and plots so a run can be audited, not just scored.

sections.heading: One model, several experiment tracks
body: The same core model is run across a few parallel tracks so results can be cross-checked rather than resting on a single configuration:
bullets: **Single-channel** — isolate what one channel can carry before scaling up.
**Multi-channel EEG** — the full scalp montage as a joint signal.
**Multi-modal** — EEG together with pupillometry, so a second physiological stream can corroborate the brain-state estimate.

sections.heading: What the system is for
body: The goal of the system is classification: turning the HLDS-derived hidden-state encodings into predictions of the condition or brain state, judged by how well those encodings separate the classes of interest. This is active research inside a collaboration, so the page stays at the level of the model and the pipeline — the HLDS and the classification goal it feeds — rather than reporting numbers.

faq.a: The state-space structure is layered so that higher-level hidden variables summarize the behavior of lower-level ones, which is what lets a small number of states stand in for many EEG channels.

faq.q: Why not just use a deep neural network?
faq.a: With limited, noisy data and a need to explain what the model is tracking, a linear dynamical system wins on interpretability and data efficiency — you can inspect the states and check that the learned dynamics are stable, which a black box does not give you.
An internal codename tied to this collaboration. I keep the specifics deliberately vague on the public site.
It tracks brain-state structure that correlates with labeled conditions. Calling that 'emotion detection' would be overclaiming what the signal supports.

glossary.definition: Electroencephalography: non-invasive measurement of brain electrical activity from the scalp.
Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System: a state-space model that represents a signal using a small set of hidden variables that change over time.
A model that explains observations using hidden variables (‘state’) plus rules for how those variables evolve over time.
An internal project codename tied to this collaboration; kept deliberately vague on the public site.

items.title: Zebrafish voltage imaging: event detection & interpretation
items.subtitle: Signal-processing pipeline for 2D voltage imaging videos that detects brief neural events and produces interpretable visual summaries.
items.imgAlt: Frame from a zebrafish voltage imaging video.
items.desc: Pipeline for 2D voltage imaging videos that flags ‘events’ (fast, localized changes) using statistical detectors inspired by radar signal processing, producing maps and summaries for downstream analysis.

details.overview: Voltage imaging produces high-frame-rate videos where brightness changes correspond (imperfectly) to changes in neural electrical activity. The practical challenge is separating true events from noise, motion, and background drift. I built and tested detectors that highlight candidate events and produce interpretable outputs for scientists to review.
what_i_built: Preprocessing routines for voltage imaging videos (normalization, background handling, and region-wise aggregation).
Event detectors that score pixels/regions over time and surface candidate events for review.
Evaluation utilities to compare detector behavior across recordings and parameter settings.
Exportable visual summaries (event maps and time-series traces) to support interpretation.
how_it_works: Treat each pixel/region as a time-series.
Estimate a baseline/noise profile from nearby frames.
Apply statistical tests to flag frames/regions whose changes are unlikely under the noise model.
Aggregate detections into event maps and interpretable summaries.

writeup.lead: Voltage imaging gives you video of neural activity — and the hard part is telling a real event apart from noise.

sections.heading: The problem: brief events in noisy video
body: Voltage imaging records fast changes in brightness that correspond, imperfectly, to electrical activity in neurons. The events you care about are short, localized, and low-contrast, sitting on top of photobleaching, motion, and sensor noise. A naive brightness threshold either drowns in false positives or misses the real thing entirely.
So the real task is not 'find bright spots' — it is 'decide, per pixel and per frame, whether a change is more surprising than the background should produce.'

sections.heading: Borrowing from radar
body: The detectors here come from radar signal processing, where the same problem — spot a faint target against a fluctuating background — has decades of theory behind it. I use CFAR-style adaptive thresholding to hold the false-alarm rate stable as the background changes, and a Quadratic Gamma Discriminator to flag deviations from a learned noise model.
Treating a microscopy problem as a detection problem is the whole idea: it means the thresholds adapt instead of being hand-tuned per recording.

figure.alt: A pixel intensity trace over time with an estimated noise band and an adaptive CFAR threshold; one spike crosses the threshold and is marked as a detected event.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — Per-pixel detection: the CFAR threshold adapts to the local noise band, so only a change that is genuinely unlikely — not merely bright — is flagged as an event.

sections.heading: The detection pipeline
body: Detection is built as a set of interchangeable stages so the pre-processing filter and the detector can be swapped and tuned independently. A parallel grid search runs across filter and detector parameters, and the best operating points are chosen by real detection-theory metrics rather than by eye.

breakdown.label: Pre-process (swap)
breakdown.text: A Gamma spatio-temporal filter for enhancement, or Kalman–MCC for robust background estimation via maximum correntropy — chosen per recording.

breakdown.label: Detect
breakdown.text: A CFAR detector scores each pixel/region over time and surfaces candidate events.

breakdown.label: Evaluate + select
breakdown.text: FROC (true-positive rate vs. false positives per image) and truncated AUC to compare detectors across the search, then top-K model summaries.

breakdown.label: Report
breakdown.text: Per-model diagnostics: event-duration histograms, FROC curves, sensitivity heatmaps, PSD comparisons, and qualitative montages.

figure.alt: Imaging video passes through an interchangeable pre-processing filter (Gamma ST or Kalman-MCC), a CFAR detector, evaluation by FROC and truncated AUC, and report generation; a parallel grid search spans the filter and detector, and a human review workbench feeds corrections back in.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — The grid-search detection pipeline. Filters and detectors are interchangeable, model selection uses detection-theory metrics, and a human review workbench closes the loop.

sections.heading: Keeping a human in the loop
body: Detectors are only half the system. A separate review workbench (a Fiji/Groovy plus browser workflow) lets a scientist inspect regions of interest and events with zoom, contrast, and overlay controls, accept/reject/mark-unsure at both the ROI and event level, and see a robust Kalman baseline under each trace. Decisions autosave, and ROI and event tables export for downstream analysis — so human judgment feeds back into which parameters win.

sections.heading: Modeling activity on a template grid
body: Beyond detection, a template-aligned 32×32 grid workflow models zebrafish left / right / neutral activity end to end: a grid autoencoder compresses each frame, a GRU predicts the latent code forward in time, and a classifier reads those latent codes — all with video-level splits so evaluation never leaks across a recording.

faq.a: Constant False Alarm Rate: a family of adaptive thresholding methods that keep false detections stable across changing noise. It is a workhorse of radar detection.
A background estimator that uses the maximum correntropy criterion instead of plain least squares, which makes it robust to the heavy-tailed noise and outliers common in imaging video.
By detection-theory metrics rather than a single accuracy number: FROC curves and truncated AUC compared across a parallel grid search, instead of a single threshold picked by eye.

faq.q: Does this run in real time?
faq.a: It is offline analysis today, built for careful review and reproducible reports, with GPU acceleration where it helps.

glossary.definition: A microscopy method that records fast changes related to electrical activity as video.
Constant False Alarm Rate: a family of adaptive thresholding methods that aim to keep false detections stable across changing noise.
Quadratic Gamma Discriminator: a statistical detector designed to highlight deviations from a learned background/noise model.

items.title: Time-series ML experiment library
items.subtitle: Reusable infrastructure for running, tracking, and comparing time-series machine learning experiments with consistent reporting.
items.imgAlt: Plot representing adaptive filtering / time-series modeling.
items.desc: Reusable experiment scaffolding for time-series ML: standardized configs, runs, metrics, and plots so model comparisons are fair and repeatable.

details.overview: Across projects, the same problem kept repeating: experiments become hard to reproduce once there are many datasets, models, and hyperparameters. This library is a practical solution: a consistent way to launch experiments, capture configuration, compute metrics, and export results.
what_i_built: A consistent ‘run’ layout (configs, outputs, plots) so results are auditable.
Utilities for sweeping model variants and hyperparameters in a controlled way.
Standardized metrics and plotting helpers for time-series tasks.
Performance-focused utilities (including GPU acceleration where appropriate) to keep iteration cycles short.
deliverables: One-command experiment runs that produce comparable outputs.
Reusable plotting and reporting utilities for papers and internal reviews.
details.status: Ongoing; shared across multiple research threads.

writeup.lead: The least glamorous project I have built, and the one that makes every other one reproducible.

sections.heading: Why build experiment infrastructure?
body: The same failure kept happening across projects: three months in, with a dozen datasets, several model variants, and a wall of hyperparameters, nobody can say exactly how a given plot was produced. This library exists to make that situation impossible.
It is a deliberately boring piece of software, and that is the point — reproducibility is not a feature you add at the end, it is a constraint you build in from the first run.

sections.heading: What a run looks like
body: Every experiment is one command that produces a self-contained run folder: the exact config that generated it, logs, computed metrics, and plots, all in a standardized layout. Two runs are always comparable because they were produced the same way, not because someone remembered to keep them consistent.

figure.alt: A config file feeds one command that produces a standardized, auditable run folder of config, logs, metrics, and plots, which makes two runs directly comparable.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — One config, one command, one auditable run folder — which is what makes comparing run A against run B honest rather than approximate.

sections.heading: A library of models behind one harness
body: The infrastructure grew out of a concrete need: comparing very different model families on the same time-series problem without the comparison quietly cheating. So alongside the run harness there is a library of adaptive and kernel filters, plus a configurable neural-network toolkit, all driven through one experiment runner.

Because every model is invoked the same way, a kernel adaptive filter and a neural network are held to identical signals and identical metrics — which is the only way a comparison between them means anything.

breakdown.label: Kernel adaptive filters
breakdown.text: QKLMS, KRLS, KRR, and Gaussian-process regression for nonlinear prediction.

breakdown.label: Functional / Wiener
breakdown.text: Functional Wiener (FWF / FWFE), the Functional Kalman Filter (FKF), ASLM, and a Wiener-filter baseline.

breakdown.label: Configurable NNs
breakdown.text: A hyperparameter-search toolkit including an information-theoretic stacked auto-encoder, run on GPU / HiPerGator.

figure.alt: Two model families — adaptive/kernel filters and configurable neural networks — feed a shared unified runner that evaluates them on benchmark chaotic signals and outputs comparable train/test MSE.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — Different model families, one harness: every model is benchmarked on the same signals with the same metric, so cross-family comparisons are honest.

sections.heading: Benchmarked on standard chaotic signals
body: Models are exercised on the classic nonlinear time-series benchmarks, where the right answer is known and difficulty is well understood:
bullets: **Mackey–Glass** — the standard delay-differential benchmark for nonlinear prediction.
**Lorenz** and **Hénon** — chaotic dynamical systems with known structure.
**Sunspot** — a real-world series for a sanity check against messy data.
Reported as **train / test MSE**, the same way for every model.

sections.heading: Design principles
body: Capture configuration; never trust memory. Standardize metrics and plotting so results line up across projects. And keep iteration fast — GPU acceleration where it helps — because infrastructure nobody wants to use does not get used.

faq.q: Is this a framework like MLflow or Weights & Biases?
faq.a: No — it is lighter and research-oriented. It is a model library plus an experiment runner for time-series work, not a general tracking service, though nothing stops you pairing it with one.

faq.q: Why benchmark on chaotic signals like Mackey–Glass?
faq.a: They are the standard proving ground for nonlinear prediction: the dynamics are known and the difficulty is well characterized, so a model's error is interpretable rather than a mystery.
The code is currently private research code rather than a released package.

glossary.definition: Data collected over time (signals, sensor streams, physiological measurements).
User-chosen settings that affect how a model trains (e.g., learning rate, window size).

items.title: Spike-train decoding with kernel least-mean-squares (KLMS)
items.subtitle: A from-scratch Python reproduction of a classic neural-decoding result: turning noisy spike trains into a continuous control signal with a kernel adaptive filter.
items.imgAlt: Diagram of spike trains feeding a KLMS decoder that reconstructs a micro-stimulation signal.
items.desc: A faithful Python reproduction of Li et al. (IEEE MLSP 2011): a spike-time RKHS KLMS decoder that maps spike trains to micro-stimulation, benchmarked against binned KLMS and GLM baselines.

details.overview: This project reproduces the core results of a well-known neural-decoding paper — Li et al., 'An adaptive decoder from spike trains to micro-stimulation using kernel least-mean-squares (KLMS)', IEEE MLSP 2011 — from scratch in Python, so the method can be understood, tested, and built on rather than taken on faith.
what_i_built: A spike-time RKHS KLMS decoder built on the cross-intensity kernel, operating directly on spike times.
A spike-time kernel APA family (KAPA / KNLMS / affine projection) with a projection-order sweep.
Binned-data baselines for comparison: a Gaussian-RBF KLMS and a Poisson-log-link GLM.
Synthetic neural-response generation with biphasic stimulation pulses, plus NMSE scoring and reconstruction plots.
how_it_works: Represent each spike train in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space via a spike-time kernel.
Learn an adaptive decoder online with kernel least-mean-squares, updating on each sample.
Reconstruct the continuous command signal and score it by normalized mean-squared error (NMSE).
Compare the spike-time decoder against binned KLMS and GLM baselines on the same synthetic data.
details.status: Synthetic reproduction implemented; rat VPL–S1 dataset sourcing in progress.

writeup.lead: A small, honest project: take a classic neural-decoding paper and rebuild its results from scratch until the numbers line up.

sections.heading: Why reproduce a 2011 paper?
body: Kernel least-mean-squares decoding of spike trains is a foundational idea in neural interfaces, and the fastest way to really understand a method is to rebuild it until it reproduces the original numbers. This project reimplements Li et al. (IEEE MLSP 2011) in Python — decoder, baselines, synthetic data, and metrics — as a clean reference I can trust and extend.
It doubles as a proving ground for the kernel-adaptive-filtering tools I use elsewhere, on a problem where the right answer is already published.

sections.heading: How the decoder works
body: Spikes are events in time, not evenly-sampled numbers, so the decoder embeds each spike train in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space using a spike-time (cross-intensity) kernel. A kernel least-mean-squares filter then learns online — updating on each sample — to map that representation to the continuous micro-stimulation command, which is scored by normalized mean-squared error.

sections.heading: Reproducing the published results
body: The point of a reproduction is the numbers, so the synthetic benchmark from the paper is rebuilt and every model is scored the same way. The spike-time kernel decoder leads the binned baselines, matching the paper's reported targets:

breakdown.label: Spike-KLMS
breakdown.text: NMSE ≈ 0.13 — the spike-time RKHS decoder, and the best of the three.

breakdown.label: Binned-KLMS
breakdown.text: NMSE ≈ 0.27 — a Gaussian-RBF KLMS on binned counts.

figure.alt: Bar chart of NMSE: Spike-KLMS about 0.13, Binned-KLMS about 0.27, Binned-GLM about 0.35 — lower is better, so the spike-time kernel decoder wins.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — Reproduced synthetic NMSE. Working directly with spike times beats binning them, as the original paper reported.

sections.heading: Where it stands
body: The synthetic reproduction is complete, including the kernel APA family and a projection-order sweep. The next step is sourcing the real rat VPL–S1 dataset used in the original study to move from synthetic validation to real recordings.

faq.a: Kernel least-mean-squares: a least-mean-squares adaptive filter applied in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space, so it can learn nonlinear mappings online while staying simple and interpretable.

faq.q: Why work with spike times instead of binned counts?
faq.a: Binning throws away temporal precision. A spike-time kernel keeps it, and the reproduction shows that this is exactly why the spike-time decoder reaches a lower error than the binned baselines.

faq.q: Is this original research or a reproduction?
faq.a: It is a faithful reproduction of a published result, built to understand and extend the method. The original work is Li et al., IEEE MLSP 2011.

glossary.definition: Kernel least-mean-squares: an adaptive filter that learns nonlinear mappings online in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space.
The sequence of firing times of a neuron, treated here as events in continuous time.
Normalized mean-squared error: reconstruction error scaled by signal power, so lower is better.
Reproducing-kernel Hilbert space: the feature space a kernel implicitly maps data into.
